Blitz — 2026 Competition Robot

FIRST Robotics Competition · Team 1771 · Robot design lead, 2026 season

12MM BALTIC BIRCH CHASSIS 420° TURRET ROTATION CNC ROUTED PID-TUNED INTAKE

Blitz is the robot I led the design of for Team 1771's 2026 season — the first time I owned the majority of a robot's architecture myself, after several years contributing CAD support to previous robots. Every subsystem below was built around one goal: survive a brutal, high-contact game without sacrificing scoring speed.

Chassis

The entire chassis is built from 12mm Baltic birch, cut on our CNC router. Wood gave us fast iteration and let us place mounting holes anywhere we needed on the fly, and we lightening-holed ("cheese-holed") the whole chassis to cut weight without sacrificing rigidity.

Intake & Hopper

The intake pivots on two motors: one drives the up-and-down motion, the other spins a row of 60-durometer composite wheels inward to pull balls in. That same pivoting motion doubles as the drive for the hopper, sliding it in and out passively as the intake moves — a fully mechanical link with no extra motor needed.

The hopper itself is polycarbonate, cut and bent on our CNC machine, and shaped to expand the effective ball storage inside the robot. The intake is PID-tuned so that a full load of balls can't push it back up on its own, which keeps that passive hopper motion reliable under game load. Both intake motors sit inside the main chassis rather than on the intake arm itself, so the entire intake can be pulled off with two bolts and reinstalled with two bolts — a deliberate call given how physically punishing this year's game was on exposed mechanisms.

Indexing — the Spindexer

Balls are indexed by what we called the spindexer: a 3D-printed cone with small holes and divots that stir the balls to prevent jams, paired with a moving polycarbonate floor attached to that cone that carries balls forward without ever compressing them. Both the cone and floor are wrapped in grip tape for consistent traction. Surrounding the moving floor is a 3D-printed ring we nicknamed the Singularity — a sloped surface that we iterated on dozens of times to stop jams and use gravity to feed balls into the moving floor faster. The whole system runs off a custom two-motor 3D-printed gearbox mounted at the bottom of the robot.

Feeder

From the bottom of the indexing system, a single-motor feeder carries balls up into the turret. Pulleys and gears set different ratios on the front and back rollers so both run correctly off that one motor. The front row uses two omni wheels to pull balls in with minimal friction, followed by a small 3D-printed ramp, then polycord that carries the balls the rest of the way up into the turret.

Turret & Shooter

The turret rotates 420 degrees, driven by two constant-force springs pulling a tether around a 3D-printed ring — a simple mechanism that gave us nearly a full rotation and a half of range. The whole assembly is 12.75 inches in diameter and carries three motors and their motor controllers directly on the turret: two drive the main shooter wheels and four back-hood shooter wheels, and one drives rotation. We spent a lot of time testing different gear ratios on the back-hood wheels specifically to balance shooting range, accuracy, and power draw.

Electronics

The electronics board sits on the bottom of the robot, protected by a metal cover that sits behind the bumpers — keeping our controllers and wiring shielded from the same contact that drove the intake's quick-swap design.

What didn't make it

We also fully CADed a climber mechanism for Blitz, but ultimately decided not to install it. Given our match strategy that season, the climber's point value didn't justify the added weight, complexity, and failure risk it would have introduced — a tradeoff call we made deliberately rather than a design that simply ran out of time.
